extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (those studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify Aristotle’s evaluative criteria for friendship, pleasure, and happiness: what counts as a good friendship, which pleasures are properly choice-worthy, and why the contemplative life is the highest form of happiness. Extracts standards and explanatory guidance from Book X of the Nicomachean Ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of friends is choice-worthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of friends is, under all circumstances, choice-worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle supports this by recommending readiness to help friends in need (without treating help as an owed right), willingness to forward their good fortune, and caution about refusing sympathy so as not to appear sullen. Friendship’s presence is intrinsically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy is most choice-worthy among friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Intimacy (communion, seeing the beloved) is to friends most choice-worthy, analogous to how sight is prized by lovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friends seek to share the things that make life desirable (drinking, hunting, studying together) because such shared activities realize intimacy. This underpins why friends wish their friends to partake in the same life-defining activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship mirrors self-regard
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is to his friend as he is to himself; thus what is choice-worthy about one’s own existence should be desired for a friend as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates friends’ desire for communion in the activities and goods that constitute a good life; it also explains why corrupt friendships spread vice while good friendships improve partners by mutual correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good friendships improve by repeated acts and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: The friendship of the good grows with intercourse; friends improve one another by repeated acts and by mutual correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes that the good take impress from one another in the points which give them pleasure; the process of repeated virtuous interaction deepens and perfects character (illustrated by poetical citation: 'Thou from the good, good things shalt surely learn').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain shape moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and Pain are primary rudders in training the young and guiding conduct; learning to like and dislike what one ought is central to forming good moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because feelings of pleasure and pain bias life-long choice, correct education in what to take pleasure in or avoid is crucial. Some advocate teaching against pleasure for pragmatic reasons, but Aristotle prefers alignment with observed facts about human motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good criterion per Eudoxus: universal aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus’s criterion: whatever all beings (rational and irrational) aim at is the Chief Good; since all aim at Pleasure, Pleasure must be the Chief Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments offered include (a) universal aiming as indicator of goodness, (b) Pleasure is chosen for its own sake (no further end), and (c) Pleasure added to other goods increases their desirability. Aristotle records these positions before criticizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-worthiness for its own sake (Eudoxian test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing that is chosen not as a means to something further but for its own sake counts as choice-worthy; Eudoxus uses this to argue Pleasure is choice-worthy in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eudoxus points to the common experience that people do not ask 'to what purpose' when pleased, implying Pleasure is intrinsically chosen. Aristotle examines limits of this test (e.g., many goods are chosen for their own sakes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound goods can outrank simple goods
rubrics_metrics.description: If adding another good (e.g., Practical Wisdom) makes a life more choice-worthy than mere Pleasure, then Pleasure alone cannot be the Chief Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s counterargument is cited: the compound life (pleasure plus wisdom) is more valuable than simple pleasure, so the simple element cannot be the maximal end. Aristotle uses this to show Eudoxus’s argument is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is a 'whole' not a Movement or Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is complete at any moment and therefore is not a Movement or a Generation (which are extended in time and divisible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues movements have duration (parts incomplete until whole achieved); pleasure resembles a complete act (like an act of sight) and so should not be classified as movement or generation. This rebuts claims that pleasure is merely a change or supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not merely a supply after pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all pleasures result from relieving a prior lack; many—mathematical pleasures, smells, sounds, memories, hopes—have no antecedent pain to be supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle rejects the notion that Pleasure is simply the filling of a deficiency (as with hunger). He distinguishes pleasures arising from genuine supplies from those intrinsic to the activity or faculty itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disgraceful pleasures are not really pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures that are disgraceful to the good are not truly pleasant, except to depraved tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that what is pleasurable to the ill-disposed should not be taken as universally pleasant—analogous to sickness altering taste or sight. Thus moral quality of the agent matters when judging whether a pleasure is genuinely good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures differ in kind according to their sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures differ in kind: those derived from honourable objects differ fundamentally from those arising from disgraceful ones; pleasures proper to intellectual activity differ from sensual pleasures, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because different faculties and activities are of different species, the pleasures that perfect them are likewise specific; this grounds qualitative distinctions between pleasures and explains why not all pleasures are equally choice-worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper pleasures perfect the corresponding Working
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure attends every percipient faculty and perfects the act of Working: the best working (best faculty on best object) yields the most perfect and most pleasant pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure is a supervening finish (like bloom in prime) that accompanies complete functioning; the pleasure both indicates and increases the quality of activity—for example, pleasure in geometry sharpens geometric work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures aid mastery and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure proper to a Working increases accuracy, endurance, and nicety of that Working—e.g., those who take pleasure in geometry become more exact geometers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses examples (music, architecture) to show that pleasure motivates deeper engagement and development of skill. This is a positive justificatory link between pleasurable engagement and excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign pleasures hinder other Workings
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures foreign to the activity in hand tend to destroy or distract from that Working, much like pains proper to a working do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: flute music distracts those engaged in conversation. When one activity’s pleasure greatly outweighs another, the pleasanter displaces the other activity, reducing overall excellence in the displaced work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures proper to bad Workings are bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Because pleasures are intimately tied to the Workings they perfect, the pleasure proper to a bad Working is itself bad; conversely pleasures proper to good Workings are good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle links moral assessment of an activity to the moral assessment of its attendant pleasure—desires for what is noble are praiseworthy; desires for the base are blameworthy. This is a criterion for judging pleasure’s moral status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is distinct from intellectual operation yet inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Although pleasure closely accompanies intellectual or perceptive operations to the extent of seeming identical, Pleasure is not an intellectual operation or a faculty of perception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes the temporal and intimate connection between activity and its pleasure but maintains a conceptual distinction: pleasure supervenes on the acting faculty rather than being the faculty's cognitive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is an activity (Working), not a mere state
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not a state (e.g., passive rest) but an activity/Working that is self-sufficient and choice-worthy for its own sake; if it were a mere state it could belong to someone who merely vegetated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle defines 'choice-worthy in itself' as lacking nothing and not being pursued for some further end. Happiness must be an active life in accordance with excellence (virtue) and therefore properly ranked among activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is not mere amusement or rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness does not consist in amusement; amusement is more like rest (adopted for preparing to work again) and not a final End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle criticizes the idea that life’s labor should aim merely at amusement. Amusement is instrumentally valuable (rest between labors) but cannot be the comprehensive End which is self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is activity in accordance with the highest Excellence (virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Happiness is a Working in the way of Excellence, then that Excellence must be the highest—namely the excellence of the best Principle (the Intellect); thus the contemplative life is the perfect Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues contemplative activity (the exercise of intellect) is highest because the intellect is supreme among internal principles, contemplation is continuous, self-sufficient, richly pleasurable in a pure way, and closer to the divine; these attributes qualify it as the best life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life’s attributes justify its primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The contemplative life is privileged because it is most continuous, contains pure and lasting pleasures, is most self-sufficient, allows 'rest' without aiming beyond itself, and approaches the divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle adds the necessary condition that a complete duration of life is needed to realize this perfection. Practical virtues are great but restless (require society, war, external goods) and so cannot equal contemplative life in self-sufficiency and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/practical virtues yield second-rank Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Lives governed by moral excellence and practical wisdom are second in degree to the contemplative life because their activities require social contexts and passions and aim beyond themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Wisdom is closely united with Moral Virtues and involves composite (mixed) nature; these activities depend more on external circumstances and passions, making them less self-sufficient and less continuously contemplative than the intellectual life.
